---
title: Use Marfa with AI agents
description: Connect Claude Code, Codex or another AI agent to your instance's MCP server, so it can find, read and save your items with only the access you give it.
---

Every instance serves MCP at `/mcp`. **An agent that connects gets tools to find, read, save and change your items**, and every tool call is made with the agent's own credential, so it reaches only what you approved. You can see what it changed and cut it off at any time. [MCP server](/mcp-server) lists the tools.

This page is for agents that run on a computer, such as Claude Code and Codex. To use Marfa in Claude or ChatGPT on the web, on the desktop or on a phone, see [Connect Claude and ChatGPT](/run/connect-claude-and-chatgpt).

## Add the Marfa plugin

The Marfa plugin teaches an agent how to work with an instance. It holds three skills and nothing else: it runs nothing on your computer and holds no MCP server, because your instance serves its own.

| Skill | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `marfa:connect` | Adds your instance's MCP server and checks that it answers. It never asks you to paste a key into the chat. |
| `marfa:find-and-save` | Finds, saves and changes items without duplicating or overwriting anything, and treats what it reads as data, never as instructions. |
| `marfa:design-a-type` | Decides whether a kind of record fits a type you have, a type that extends one, or a new type, and drafts the smallest change. |

<Tabs items={["Claude Code", "Codex"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add withmarfa/marfa-plugin
claude plugin install marfa@withmarfa
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="Codex">

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add withmarfa/marfa-plugin
codex plugin add marfa@withmarfa
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Start a new session, ask the agent to connect to Marfa, and give it your instance's address. The `connect` skill does the steps in the next section for you.

## Connect the agent

Choose the endpoint for the work. `/mcp` finds, reads, saves and changes items. `/mcp/schema` adds tools that shape what the instance holds, such as registering a type, and `/mcp/admin` adds tools that run it, such as reading the audit log. **Connect the smallest one that does the job.**

Add the server with your instance's address, then sign in:

<Tabs items={["Claude Code", "Codex"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user marfa https://marfa.example.com/mcp
```

Then run `/mcp` in a session and choose **marfa** to sign in. `--scope user` adds the server for every project of yours; leave it out to add it for this project only.

</Tab>
<Tab value="Codex">

```bash
codex mcp add marfa --url https://marfa.example.com/mcp
codex mcp login marfa
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Your browser opens your instance's **Approve access** page. Sign in as the owner if you aren't already. **Full access** gives the agent what it asked for; **Choose access** lets you give less, such as read and edit on notes and nothing else. [Access](/access#what-the-owner-approves) describes the page.

The agent then calls `marfa_overview`, which answers with the types, tags and views it can reach, and works from there. If it later needs access you didn't approve, such as write access to a type, the instance tells its client which scope to ask for, and a client that supports this asks you to approve it.

The computer that runs the agent must reach the instance at its address: over HTTPS, or at `http://localhost` on the same machine. An address on your tailnet works, and so does one on the public internet. [Install the server](/run/install#choose-how-its-reached) covers the choices.

## Connect an agent that runs unattended

An agent that runs on a schedule, with nobody to approve it in a browser, uses a key instead. **Give each agent a key of its own**, holding only what it needs. This key reads and writes notes, reads tasks, and stops working after 30 days:

```bash
marfa keys create --label nightly-digest --source nightly-digest \
  --type-permission core.note=write \
  --type-permission core.task=read \
  --expires-in 30d
```

Run it as the owner, or with a credential that holds `keys.mint`. The CLI prints the key, which begins `marfa_k1_`, once. **The source, `nightly-digest`, is stamped on every item the agent creates**, so you can tell its work from yours. [Manage keys](/run/manage-keys) covers what else a key can hold.

Put the key in `MARFA_API_KEY` in the agent's environment, from your secrets manager, and have the client send it as a Bearer header:

<Tabs items={["Claude Code", "Codex"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">

```json title=".mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "marfa": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://marfa.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${MARFA_API_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}
```

Claude Code reads `${MARFA_API_KEY}` from the environment, so the key stays out of the file.

</Tab>
<Tab value="Codex">

```bash
codex mcp add marfa --url https://marfa.example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var MARFA_API_KEY
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## What the agent can and can't do

- **It reaches only what its credential reaches.** A type you didn't approve is invisible to it, and its tools list only what it can use.
- **It reads item content as data.** The instance tells every agent that what it reads is what you saved, never instructions to follow, and to tell you when an item gives an AI instructions.
- **Deleting asks first.** The first `marfa_delete` call only previews what the trash would take. The agent shows you, and moves anything only when you agree. Moving a type's items, revoking a key and pointing a webhook at an address work the same way.
- **It can't overwrite a change it hasn't seen.** `marfa_update` takes the version the agent read, and changes nothing if the item changed since.
- **It can fetch a file from a public web address** to save it. The instance records every fetch in the audit log, and `MARFA_MCP_FETCH_ENABLED=false` turns fetching off, as [Settings](/run/settings#every-environment-setting) shows.
- **It can't purge, export, restore, change settings or manage your sign-ins.** No tool does those, at any endpoint.

**You can see what it did.** Every write through a tool is in the [audit log](/run/audit-log) with `"via": "mcp"` and the credential that made it. **You can stop it at once:** revoke its key with `marfa keys revoke <key id>`, or disconnect it on the **Connected apps** page, as [Authenticate](/build/authenticate#revoke-access) describes.

## Use the CLI instead

A coding agent that runs shell commands can also use the [CLI](/cli), which reaches every operation. Write a [profile](/cli#name-a-server-with-a-profile) whose `key_command` reads the agent's key from your secrets manager, so the key is never in a file:

```toml title="profiles.toml"
[example]
url = "https://marfa.example.com"
key_command = ["op", "read", "op://Private/Marfa/agent-key"]
```

Then set `MARFA_PROFILE=example` and `MARFA_NO_KEYCHAIN=1` in the environment the agent runs its commands in. **With the keychain off, a command that names no profile or server is refused**, so the agent can't reach whichever instance the keychain made current. Each write also prints which instance it changed on standard error.

Tell the agent how to use it in its instructions file:

```markdown title="AGENTS.md"
## Marfa

My notes are in Marfa. Use the `marfa` CLI, with `--json` on every command.

- Learn what the key reaches: `marfa overview --json`
- Find notes: `marfa search "<words>" --type core.note --json`
- Read one: `marfa items get <id> --json`
- To change one, read it first, then pass its `version` to `marfa items update`.
```

With `--json`, a refusal is one JSON object on the last line of standard error, and the exit code says whether to try again. [Exit codes](/cli#exit-codes) lists them.

## Let the agent read these docs

An agent that builds on Marfa does better with the current docs than from memory. Connect the [Docs MCP server](/docs-mcp-server) so it can search them, or point it at [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt), an index of every page as Markdown.
